docs.title: La Grenouillère
docs.text: La Grenouillère by Claude Monet. Category: landscape. Tags: impressionist, water, outdoor, reflections. Monet and Renoir sat side by side at this floating café near Paris in 1869, inventing Impressionism's signature loose, sun-dappled touch. Short, broken comma-strokes laid side by side — Monet and Renoir were learning to let color mix in the eye rather than on the palette.

docs.title: Water Lilies (Agapanthus)
docs.text: Water Lilies (Agapanthus) by Claude Monet. Category: landscape. Tags: impressionist, water, flowers, soft, blue, green. One of Monet's monumental late 'Water Lilies,' painted nearly blind, dissolving the boundary between water, sky, and reflected light. Broad, sweeping arcs applied with wide brushes; at this scale individual strokes dissolve into shimmering atmosphere rather than form.

docs.title: Garden at Sainte-Adresse
docs.text: Garden at Sainte-Adresse by Claude Monet. Category: landscape. Tags: impressionist, outdoor, colorful, garden, sea, bright. Monet's boldly modern terrace scene at Sainte-Adresse—flat planes and dazzling coastal sun borrowed straight from Japanese woodblock prints. Flat, nearly even passages of paint borrowed from Japanese woodblock prints — Monet suppressed modelling to make the scene read as pure color.

docs.title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
docs.text: Wheat Field with Cypresses by Vincent van Gogh. Category: landscape. Tags: expressionist, landscape, nature, swirling, yellow, green. Painted from the Saint-Rémy asylum grounds, the swirling cypresses translate Van Gogh's emotional intensity directly into color and rhythm. Vigorous, spiraling strokes follow the contours of each form — sky, cypress, and hills are all woven from the same restless rhythm.

docs.title: Irises
docs.text: Irises by Vincent van Gogh. Category: abstract. Tags: expressionist, flowers, purple, bold, yellow, green. One of Van Gogh's last paintings at Saint-Rémy, the irises pulse with energy yet feel unusually serene compared to his turbulent final months. Thick impasto applied in directional dabs that map onto petals and leaves, giving the surface a physical weight the color alone could not achieve.

docs.title: Self-Portrait with a Straw Hat
docs.text: Self-Portrait with a Straw Hat by Vincent van Gogh. Category: portrait. Tags: expressionist, portrait, blue, orange, bold. One of thirty self-portraits Van Gogh made in Paris, each an experiment—here he tests Pointillism and a palette that would define his mature style. Small Pointillist dots of complementary color — Van Gogh was experimenting with Seurat's method, placing pure hues next to each other for optical vibration.

docs.title: Oleanders
docs.text: Oleanders by Vincent van Gogh. Category: abstract. Tags: expressionist, flowers, red, pink, bold, warm. Painted in Arles with deliberate symbolism: Van Gogh saw the oleander as a plant of life, paired with Zola's novel on joy and sorrow. Bold, confident strokes applied wet-into-wet; the oleander blossoms are built from single loaded brushmarks rather than careful blended shading.

docs.title: The Dancing Class
docs.text: The Dancing Class by Edgar Degas. Category: portrait. Tags: impressionist, figure, indoor, dance, warm, white. Degas showed ballet as grueling labor—tired dancers wait, the ballet master watches—not the polished spectacle audiences paid to see. Short diagonal hatching strokes define the dancers' tutus with almost no blending — Degas wanted the sensation of light catching fabric, not the fabric itself.

docs.title: By the Seashore
docs.text: By the Seashore by Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Category: portrait. Tags: impressionist, portrait, blue, outdoor, woman. Renoir's atmospheric portrait of an unknown woman on the Normandy coast, her identity still disputed by art historians a century later. Long, fluid strokes in the background contrast with the precise rendering of the sitter's face, showing Renoir's Impressionist looseness outside the focal point.

docs.title: Madame Georges Charpentier and Her Children
docs.text: Madame Georges Charpentier and Her Children by Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Category: portrait. Tags: impressionist, portrait, interior, dark, family. This Salon triumph made Renoir fashionable overnight; Marguerite Charpentier's literary salon was the social engine of Paris in the 1870s. Smooth, finished brushwork that satisfied the Salon — Renoir suppressed his Impressionist instinct here to produce the even surface academic juries rewarded.

docs.title: Aristotle with a Bust of Homer
docs.text: Aristotle with a Bust of Homer by Rembrandt van Rijn. Category: portrait. Tags: baroque, portrait, dark, gold, dramatic. Rembrandt imagined Aristotle contemplating Homer's bust, his hand resting on a chain given by his patron Alexander the Great—a meditation on fame and thought. Rembrandt's glazing technique: dozens of thin transparent layers built up over weeks, the final surface lit from within rather than painted on top.

docs.title: View of Toledo
docs.text: View of Toledo by El Greco. Category: landscape. Tags: mannerist, dramatic, dark, green, stormy. El Greco's only surviving pure landscape crackles with a supernatural storm that never visits real Toledo—pure spiritual theater above the city. El Greco's elongated strokes twist with a flickering energy that turns paint into pure spiritual light rather than observed fact.

docs.title: Still Life with Apples and Pears
docs.text: Still Life with Apples and Pears by Paul Cézanne. Category: abstract. Tags: post-impressionist, still-life, colorful, fruits. Cézanne's obsessive still lifes broke perspective open with multiple viewpoints and tilted planes, handing Picasso the key to Cubism. Horizontal and vertical strokes of similar weight that deliberately flatten and shift perspective — the foundation of every Cubist painting to come.

docs.title: The Englishman at the Moulin Rouge
docs.text: The Englishman at the Moulin Rouge by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec. Category: portrait. Tags: post-impressionist, urban, night, vivid, orange, figures. Lautrec documented Paris nightlife as both insider and outsider, his lithographic style compressing figures into bold outlines that shaped modern graphic design. Lautrec used the rough grain of cardboard as part of his brushwork, letting the surface texture break up his strokes into a lithographic dot pattern.

docs.title: Ia Orana Maria (Hail Mary)
docs.text: Ia Orana Maria (Hail Mary) by Paul Gauguin. Category: portrait. Tags: post-impressionist, tropical, warm, figures, colorful. Gauguin's first Tahitian masterpiece reimagines the Virgin and Child as Polynesian islanders—faith, colonialism, and longing in a single canvas. Broad decorative passages of color with minimal modelling, influenced by Polynesian tapa cloth patterns — Gauguin was moving toward flat symbolic color.

docs.title: The Card Players
docs.text: The Card Players by Paul Cézanne. Category: portrait. Tags: post-impressionist, figures, warm, dark, interior. The most intimate of Cézanne's five 'Card Players' versions, distilling rural Provençal farmers into monumental, almost sculptural forms. Heavy, almost sculptural impasto applied with a palette knife as much as a brush — Cézanne was building form through color weight, not line.

docs.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
docs.text: The Great Wave off Kanagawa by Katsushika Hokusai. Category: landscape. Tags: japanese, woodblock, water, bold, blue, dynamic. Published by Hokusai around age 70, the great wave dwarfs Mount Fuji deliberately—the sea, not the mountain, is sovereign. Woodblock printing, not painting: Hokusai's contour lines are cut into wood and printed in registration, the 'strokes' are carved grooves filled with ink.

docs.title: Young Woman with a Water Pitcher
docs.text: Young Woman with a Water Pitcher by Johannes Vermeer. Category: portrait. Tags: dutch-golden-age, portrait, quiet, blue, soft, light. Vermeer's quiet interior captures northern light as liquid; the subject's identity and the action's meaning are both left deliberately open. Invisible layered glazes over a detailed underpainting — Vermeer's surface shows almost no individual brushmarks, just accumulated light.

docs.title: Madame X (Madame Pierre Gautreau)
docs.text: Madame X (Madame Pierre Gautreau) by John Singer Sargent. Category: portrait. Tags: portrait, elegant, black, pale, dramatic, woman. Sargent's portrait of Madame Gautreau scandalized Paris in 1884; her pale skin and bold posture were read as flagrantly sexual. Rapid, confident strokes applied in a single sitting — Sargent's virtuoso technique built the entire figure from wide sweeping marks that look effortless but hide enormous skill.

docs.title: Juan de Pareja
docs.text: Juan de Pareja by Diego Velázquez. Category: portrait. Tags: baroque, portrait, dark, dramatic, man. Velázquez painted his enslaved assistant Juan de Pareja with such psychological presence that the portrait was exhibited before the artist's own work. Long, tapering strokes that follow the weave of the canvas; Velázquez left individual brushmarks visible at a distance, presaging Manet by two centuries.

docs.title: The Gulf Stream
docs.text: The Gulf Stream by Winslow Homer. Category: landscape. Tags: american, ocean, dramatic, blue, tropical. Homer's Black sailor adrift on a dismasted boat surrounded by sharks drew no sympathy when exhibited—its politics were ahead of its time. Homer's watercolor-influenced oil technique: thin, translucent washes of blue-green laid over a chalky underpainting to make the sea glow from below.

docs.title: Snap the Whip
docs.text: Snap the Whip by Winslow Homer. Category: landscape. Tags: american, outdoor, green, children, summer, bright. Homer captured the kinetic joy of a boys' game in the Catskills, turning an everyday moment into a hymn to post-Civil War American childhood. Quick, calligraphic strokes that capture movement rather than anatomy — Homer painted the action itself, not the boys performing it.

docs.title: Washington Crossing the Delaware
docs.text: Washington Crossing the Delaware by Emanuel Leutze. Category: landscape. Tags: american, historical, dramatic, blue, figures, ice. Leutze painted this heroic crossing in Düsseldorf, his ice-choked Delaware populated by German models—American myth made in Germany. Academic, fully blended passages designed to look finished rather than painted — Leutze wanted heroic drama, not visible process.

docs.title: Young Mother Sewing
docs.text: Young Mother Sewing by Mary Cassatt. Category: portrait. Tags: impressionist, portrait, soft, interior, woman, child. Cassatt centers the unglamorous intimacy of motherhood: a woman sews while a child leans against her, ignoring the viewer completely. Broken Impressionist strokes in the background with a tighter touch on the figures — Cassatt followed Degas in giving interiors the same vigorous surface as outdoor scenes.

docs.title: A Young Girl Reading
docs.text: A Young Girl Reading by Jean-Honoré Fragonard. Category: portrait. Tags: rococo, portrait, yellow, warm, soft, woman. Fragonard's girl is entirely absorbed in her book—a radical act of interiority in an era when women's minds were rarely taken seriously by painters. Rococo feathered strokes that give the dress and cushion an airy insubstantiality — paint thick enough to catch the light, thin enough to seem like breath.

docs.title: Haystacks (Effect of Snow and Sun)
docs.text: Haystacks (Effect of Snow and Sun) by Claude Monet. Category: landscape. Tags: impressionist, landscape, warm, orange, snow, sunset. Haystacks in changing light became Monet's first series—the subject is almost irrelevant; it is time itself being painted. Parallel horizontal strokes in the sky and earth contrasted with textured impasto on the haystack itself — the subject is paint responding to light.

docs.title: The Olive Trees
docs.text: The Olive Trees by Vincent van Gogh. Category: landscape. Tags: expressionist, landscape, green, swirling, nature. Van Gogh's olive trees twist with the same restless energy as his cypresses—nature as felt, not merely seen. Short, swirling strokes follow the twist of each branch — Van Gogh mapped observed motion onto the surface of the canvas like a seismograph.

docs.title: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ohashi Bridge
docs.text: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ohashi Bridge by Utagawa Hiroshige. Category: landscape. Tags: japanese, woodblock, rain, blue, dark, dramatic. Hiroshige's rain lines are almost calligraphic; this print so impressed Van Gogh that he painted two oil copies of it. Woodblock printing: the rain is thin parallel lines cut into a separate block and overprinted in black — a technique Van Gogh tried to replicate in oil.

docs.title: Plum Park in Kameido
docs.text: Plum Park in Kameido by Utagawa Hiroshige. Category: landscape. Tags: japanese, woodblock, red, bold, spring, branch. A close-cropped plum branch in crimson—Hiroshige's bold framing directly inspired Degas and the Impressionists' asymmetric compositions. Bold flat color fields separated by ink outlines — no modelling or shadow, just the silhouette of each element acting as pure shape.

docs.title: The Rocky Mountains, Lander's Peak
docs.text: The Rocky Mountains, Lander's Peak by Albert Bierstadt. Category: landscape. Tags: american, landscape, mountains, blue, green, majestic. Bierstadt's theatrical light turns the Rockies into a sublime stage set, performing Manifest Destiny as landscape painting. Smooth blended passages in the dramatic sky with tighter, more textured work in the foreground rocks — a Hudson River technique for making distance feel infinite.

docs.title: The Oxbow (View from Mount Holyoke)
docs.text: The Oxbow (View from Mount Holyoke) by Thomas Cole. Category: landscape. Tags: american, landscape, river, green, lush, dramatic. Cole painted himself as a tiny figure in the lower right, reminding us that the artist—like nature—is both part of and apart from the sublime. Layered glazes over a toned ground, with visible impasto only in the sunlit passages — Cole used Old Master technique to paint New World wilderness.

docs.title: Woman with a Lute
docs.text: Woman with a Lute by Johannes Vermeer. Category: portrait. Tags: dutch-golden-age, portrait, quiet, blue, soft, music. Vermeer's woman pauses mid-tune, gazing toward window light—a frozen moment of private music that feels more like a memory than a painting. Ultra-fine stippling in the lit areas combined with smooth fluid passages in shadow — Vermeer used different brushes for each zone of luminosity.

docs.title: Piazza San Marco
docs.text: Piazza San Marco by Canaletto. Category: landscape. Tags: venetian, architecture, blue-sky, crowded, city. Canaletto's veduta were sold as souvenirs to Grand Tour travelers; his Venice is real and theatrical simultaneously. Thin, even paint over a precise architectural underdrawing — Canaletto used a camera obscura to project the scene, then painted almost like a printer filling in plates.

docs.title: Portrait of a Man
docs.text: Portrait of a Man by Frans Hals. Category: portrait. Tags: dutch-golden-age, portrait, dark, white-collar, expressive. Hals captured his sitter's psychological vitality with brushwork so loose and alive that it anticipates Manet by two centuries. Slashing, rapid strokes applied wet-into-wet in a single session — Hals refused to rework passages, so the brushmarks preserve exactly the speed and pressure of his hand.

docs.title: Ballet Rehearsal on the Set
docs.text: Ballet Rehearsal on the Set by Edgar Degas. Category: portrait. Tags: impressionist, dance, figures, warm, indoor, pastel. A rehearsal, not a performance—Degas preferred the unglamorous preparation, the waiting, the disciplined repetition that produced the illusion of effortless grace. Short hatching strokes in pastel over a monotype base — Degas built up his surfaces through layered dry media rather than the liquid brushwork of his Impressionist peers.

docs.title: Tahitian Women on the Beach
docs.text: Tahitian Women on the Beach by Paul Gauguin. Category: portrait. Tags: post-impressionist, tropical, warm, figures, orange, colorful. Gauguin's Tahitian women occupy the picture plane with quiet authority, indifferent to the colonial gaze that funded the painting. Large flat planes of saturated color with no blending — Gauguin wanted the picture to read as symbolic color fields, not as modelled flesh.

docs.title: Wisteria
docs.text: Wisteria by Claude Monet. Category: abstract. Tags: impressionist, flowers, purple, lavender, soft. Monet painted wisteria nearly blind, working at close range—the blooms dissolve into pure color fields that anticipate Abstract Expressionism. Working nearly blind, Monet applied paint in broad arcs guided by touch as much as sight — the result is more tactile than visual, pure color without contour.

docs.title: A Girl Asleep
docs.text: A Girl Asleep by Johannes Vermeer. Category: portrait. Tags: dutch-golden-age, portrait, warm, interior, brown, quiet. Vermeer's first genre scene: a maid slumped over a table—ambiguous between sleep, grief, and intoxication—painted with radiant Dutch light. Loose, fluid strokes in the background tablecloth contrast with the tightly rendered face — an early work where Vermeer was still developing his characteristic stillness.

docs.title: At the Circus Fernando: The Ringmaster
docs.text: At the Circus Fernando: The Ringmaster by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec. Category: portrait. Tags: post-impressionist, circus, figures, vivid, orange, dark. Lautrec cropped the circus ring radically, placing us inside the action—an angle no academic painter would dare. Rapid calligraphic strokes that summarize a pose in a few marks — Lautrec could capture a performer's gesture in the time it took to make it.

docs.title: Northeaster
docs.text: Northeaster by Winslow Homer. Category: landscape. Tags: american, ocean, dramatic, dark, waves, stormy. Homer painted this Prout's Neck scene multiple times, returning to the Atlantic's raw power as if it held an answer he couldn't yet articulate. Homer scraped wet paint with a palette knife to create the foam's texture, then painted transparent washes over it — the sea is built as much by removing paint as applying it.
